title: Indexes and access methods
one_liner: An index is a side structure that maps column values to heap row locations (TIDs), reached through a plug-in API so btree, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, BRIN and hash all work the same way.
analogy: A book index: you look up a word, get page numbers (TIDs), then flip to those pages (heap) to read the real text.
big_picture: An index stores keys plus TIDs. A TID is a (block, offset) address of a row in the table.
Every index type is a plug-in. It fills one IndexAmRoutine struct of function pointers (amapi.h).
The planner asks each index's amcostestimate how expensive a scan is, then picks the cheapest plan.
At run time the executor calls amgettuple to get TIDs one by one, or amgetbitmap to get many at once.
The table AM turns a TID into a visible row. Heap checks the snapshot (MVCC), so the index never holds visibility.
Index entries can point at dead rows. VACUUM removes them via ambulkdelete.

flow.detail: For each table, it lists its indexes, then builds an IndexPath for each one whose columns match the WHERE clause.
cost_index calls the AM's amcostestimate (btcostestimate for btree). Cheapest path wins against seq scan and bitmap scan.
IndexNext usually opens the scan lazily on the first call, with index_beginscan. That reaches the AM ambeginscan and the table AM index_scan_begin.

flow.step: Ask the index for the next TID
flow.detail: tableam_index_getnext_tid calls amgettuple. The AM stores the TID in scan->xs_heaptid.
First call goes _bt_first, which uses _bt_search to descend from root to a leaf. Later calls use _bt_next to walk along the leaf.
The heap table AM reads the heap page and walks the HOT chain to find a version visible to the snapshot.
If xs_recheck is set (lossy index), the executor re-tests the quals. Then the row goes up the plan tree.

flow.step: Inserts keep the index in sync
flow.detail: On INSERT the executor calls index_insert, which calls aminsert. For btree that is _bt_doinsert, which may split a page and write WAL.

diagram.claim: A query goes from planner cost choice, through the generic index AM API into btree, then via the table AM to a visible heap row.

interview.q: What is an index, and what does it store?
answer: A separate on-disk structure with key values plus TIDs.
A TID is the (block number, offset) of a heap row.
It speeds up lookups so we skip reading the whole table.
interview.trap: Indexes do not hold full rows or visibility info. Visibility lives in the heap.

interview.q: How does Postgres support so many index types?
answer: Each type has a handler function, like bthandler in nbtree.c, that returns an IndexAmRoutine.
The struct holds function pointers: ambuild, aminsert, amgettuple, amgetbitmap, amcostestimate and more.
Core code calls only those pointers via indexam.c, so it never needs to know the type.
Flags like amcanorder and amcanunique tell the planner what the AM can do.

interview.q: Why does CREATE INDEX call ambuild, and aminsert is different?
answer: ambuild bulk-loads from a whole heap scan, e.g. btbuild sorts all keys first (nbtsort.c).
aminsert adds one entry per new row, e.g. btinsert.
Bulk build is much faster than inserting row by row.

interview.q: Walk me through an index scan, from plan to row.
answer: IndexNext in nodeIndexscan.c opens the scan with index_beginscan.
It calls table_index_getnext_slot, which runs the table AM's callback.
That callback calls amgettuple to get a TID, then fetches the heap tuple.
If the tuple is visible and passes the recheck, it is returned.
Older branches (PG17 and earlier) use different names: index_getnext_slot and index_fetch_heap.
interview.trap: The index AM does not read the heap. The table AM does that part.

interview.q: How does btree find a key?
answer: _bt_search walks from the root down internal pages to a leaf, using _bt_binsrch on each page.
_bt_moveright steps right if a concurrent split moved the key.
_bt_first then positions inside the leaf, and _bt_readpage (in nbtreadpage.c) collects matches.
_bt_next follows right-links to continue the scan.
interview.trap: btree is not a classic B-tree. It is Lehman-Yao, with right-links and high keys so readers need no big locks.

interview.q: What happens when a btree leaf page is full?
answer: _bt_insertonpg first tries to make room (dedup via _bt_dedup_pass, or delete dead items).
If that fails, _bt_split makes a new right sibling and picks a split point (nbtsplitloc.c).
The parent gets a new downlink. All of it is WAL logged so crash recovery can redo it.
Splits are done in two steps, so readers can still reach keys by the right-link.

interview.q: When do GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, BRIN and hash beat btree?
answer: GIN: many keys per row, like arrays, jsonb, full text. Key maps to a posting list of TIDs.
GiST: generic tree for overlap and nearest-neighbor, like geometry. Uses penalty and picksplit support functions.
SP-GiST: space-partitioning trees like quad-trees and tries, with inner and leaf tuples.
BRIN: tiny, stores summaries (min/max) per page range. Great for naturally ordered huge tables.
hash: only equality, buckets with overflow pages.
interview.trap: Hash indexes are not just a faster btree. They cannot do range queries or ordering.

interview.q: Why can an index scan be skipped even when an index exists?
answer: Planner costs it with amcostestimate, and seq scan may be cheaper if many rows match.
Bitmap scans use amgetbitmap to collect TIDs first, then read heap in page order.
Stale statistics, non-matching operator classes, or non-immutable expressions also block use.
interview.trap: Having an index never forces its use. The cost model decides.

interview.q: How does this tie to the table AM API?
answer: TableAmRoutine in tableam.h lets heap or another storage plug in.
It has index_scan_begin, index_scan_reset, index_scan_end, and fetch_tid.
The table AM sets scan->xs_getnext_slot, so each table type decides how a TID becomes a visible row.
Heap's version, heapam_index_heap_fetch, walks the HOT chain with heap_hot_search_buffer.

contributor_tips: Read src/backend/access/nbtree/README first, then follow _bt_first and _bt_search in nbtsearch.c with a debugger.
Learn IndexAmRoutine by reading src/test/modules/dummy_index_am and contrib/bloom, which are small example AMs.
Use contrib/amcheck to verify btree changes. Index code must also write correct WAL and pass recovery tests.
Be careful with buffer locks and pins. Mistakes here cause rare deadlocks or corrupt indexes, not clean failures.

glossary.meaning: Tuple identifier: heap block number plus offset, the row's address.
A plug-in implementing an index type, or table storage.
Heap-only tuple versions linked on one page, so no new index entry is needed.
A list of TIDs that share one key, used by GIN and btree dedup.
Index may return false matches, so quals are re-tested on the real row.
Collect TIDs into a bitmap, then read the heap in page order.

more: Index-only scans skip the heap when the visibility map says the page is all-visible.
Bitmap scans have their own executor nodes (nodeBitmapIndexscan.c, nodeBitmapHeapscan.c).
Operator classes decide what a column can be indexed with.
Multicolumn indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule. Partial, expression and INCLUDE indexes exist too.
HOT updates avoid new index entries when no indexed column changes.
